title: 22. Interview: Object Storage
summary: Interview Q&A for Object Storage — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Object Storage interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Why does object storage use a flat namespace instead of a directory hierarchy, and how does this enable virtually unlimited scale?
**Answer:** A flat namespace means there is no parent-child directory tree to traverse, lock, or keep consistent — every object is addressed by a single opaque key, and lookup is a single hash table probe. This eliminates the inode tree, directory locks, and rename coordination that make POSIX filesystems hard to shard. Without those constraints, the index can be partitioned by consistent hashing across thousands of nodes, and adding capacity is just "add another node, rebalance a slice of keys" with no impact on existing lookups. The "directories" users see (e.g. `movies/Inception/1080p.mp4`) are just conventions on key prefixes; a LIST with a prefix filter is a string-range scan, not a tree walk. S3's bucket holds tens of billions of objects in a single flat namespace for exactly this reason — the system has no notion of "directory depth" or "folder permissions" to enforce, so it can scale horizontally without bound. The trade-off is that operations that need true hierarchy (atomic rename of a subtree, directory-level permissions, recursive listing with consistency) are either impossible or eventually consistent.
**Visual:**
```
filesystem:   /a/b/c/d.txt -> 4 inode lookups + locks
object store: key="a/b/c/d.txt" -> 1 hash probe, no locks
scale:        add node -> hash ring rebalances a slice, others untouched
```

### Q2. What is the difference between availability, durability, and consistency as they apply to S3, and why does S3's SLA quote 11 nines for one but not the others?
**Answer:** Durability is the probability that a byte written will still be retrievable a year later (S3 Standard: 99.999999999% — i.e., you expect to lose 1 object per 10,000,000,000 stored per year). Availability is the probability that a GET issued right now will succeed (S3 SLA: 99.9%–99.99% depending on tier). Consistency is whether a read reflects the latest write — S3 has been strongly consistent for reads-after-writes since December 2020, but LIST operations can still lag the most recent PUT by a few seconds because the index is updated asynchronously. The reason the headline number is durability is the architecture: erasure coding across 11+9 disks in 3+ AZs means that to lose an object you must lose enough disks simultaneously that the math drops below the reconstruction threshold, which happens with probability ~1e-11. Availability is bounded by the simpler problem of keeping the HTTP front-end up, which is 99.99% on a good day because of DNS, network, and operational issues. Consistency is now strong for the common case but eventually consistent for some operations because the index and data planes are decoupled for throughput.
**Visual:**
```
Durability (11 nines):  erasure 11+9 across 3 AZs -> P(loss) ~ 1e-11
Availability (4 nines): HTTP FE uptime -> ~52 min downtime/year
Consistency:            read-after-write STRONG (since 2020)
                        LIST-after-write  EVENTUAL (index async)
```

### Q3. How does S3's erasure coding compare to replication in terms of storage overhead and durability, and why did S3 move from one to the other?
**Answer:** Replication stores N full copies, so 3x replication costs 3x storage and survives any 2 simultaneous disk failures. Erasure coding splits an object into k data chunks and m parity chunks, any k of which suffice to reconstruct the object — so 11+9 (k=11, m=9) survives 9 simultaneous failures for 1.82x storage overhead, versus 3x for the same durability with 3x replication. The math: with 3x replication you survive 2 failures; to survive 9 failures via replication you'd need 10x overhead. S3 originally used 2+1 triple replication (3x overhead, survive 2 failures) and around 2015–2016 migrated to 11+9 Reed-Solomon across multiple AZs (1.82x overhead, survive 9 failures) — same durability, ~40% storage cost reduction. The trade-off is CPU and latency: reconstructing an object from parity requires reading 11 chunks and doing matrix math, while replication just reads one chunk, so reads are slower for cold objects. S3 hides this with full-object replicas for hot objects and on-the-fly reconstruction for cold ones, and the storage savings more than pay for the extra CPU.
**Visual:**
```
3x replication:  A B C   (3 copies, survive 2 failures, 3x cost)
11+9 erasure:    D1..D11 P1..P9  (any 11 of 20 reconstructs, survive 9, 1.82x cost)
to survive 9 failures via replication -> need 10x copies (10x cost)
```

### Q4. When should you use object storage versus block storage versus file storage, and what is the canonical failure mode if you pick wrong?
**Answer:** Object storage is right for "data at rest" that is written once and read many times in whole or in byte range — backups, ML datasets, container images, data lake partitions, static web assets, log archives. Block storage is right for workloads that need random reads and writes at low latency — a database's primary storage, a VM's boot disk, an OLTP system's WAL. File storage is right when multiple clients need shared POSIX access to the same namespace — a NAS for development teams, a shared config directory, ML training scripts that many GPU nodes mount. The canonical failure modes are: using object storage for a database (S3 GET latency is 20–50ms, far too slow for OLTP, and there is no append or partial write); using block storage for a data lake (EBS is bound to one AZ, costs 3x S3, and is not shareable across instances); using file storage for petabyte-scale backups (EFS is 10x the cost of S3 Glacier and not designed for write-once archives). The mental model is "is this actively being computed on?" — if yes, block or file; if no, object.
**Visual:**
```
data at rest, big, durable, slow      -> object  (S3)
active compute, random R/W, low lat   -> block   (EBS)
shared mount, POSIX, many readers     -> file    (EFS)
wrong pick = 10x cost OR 1000x latency
```

### Q5. How does S3 achieve strong read-after-write consistency, and what operations remain eventually consistent?
**Answer:** Before December 2020 S3 was only eventually consistent for overwrites and deletes — a PUT followed by a GET could return either the old or the new version, which broke many applications that assumed atomicity. AWS fixed this by re-architecting the metadata index to be the source of truth for the latest version: every PUT/DELETE writes a new version record to a strongly-consistent key-value store (built on their internal Aurora-style log), and the GET path consults this store first before reading the data plane. The data plane remains eventually consistent (erasure-coded fragments land on disks asynchronously), but reads are routed to the version pointed at by the index, so the user always sees the latest write. Operations that remain eventually consistent: LIST-after-PUT (the listing index is updated asynchronously, so a freshly-PUT key may not appear in a LIST for 1–3 seconds); cross-region replication (a PUT in us-east-1 takes seconds to minutes to appear in the replica bucket); and Glacier restores (restoring an archived object takes minutes to hours). The lesson is that "strong consistency" is a property of a specific operation on a specific API, not of the system as a whole.
**Visual:**
```
PUT k=v -> strong index update (version N+1)
GET k   -> consult index -> version N+1 -> read data plane at v's location
LIST    -> reads listing index, async -> may miss k for ~1s
```

### Q6. What are S3 storage classes, and how do you decide which to use for a given workload?
**Answer:** S3 Standard is for hot data — ~$0.023/GB-month, millisecond access, 99.99% availability. S3 Standard-IA (Infrequent Access) is for data accessed monthly or less — ~$0.0125/GB-month, same latency, but a $0.01/GB retrieval fee. S3 One-Zone-IA is the same price as IA but stores in one AZ (99.5% availability, lower durability) — for re-creatable data like derivative thumbnails. S3 Glacier Instant Archive is $0.004/GB-month, same latency as IA. S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval (formerly S3 Glacier) is $0.0036/GB-month, retrieval takes minutes to hours. S3 Glacier Deep Archive is $0.00099/GB-month (cheaper than a tape), retrieval takes 12 hours. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between tiers based on access patterns for a small monitoring fee. The decision rule: if you read it >1x/month, Standard; if <1x/month, IA; if <1x/year, Glacier Flexible; if never (compliance archive), Deep Archive. The hidden cost is retrieval fees — accessing 1TB of IA costs $10 in retrieval fees on top of the bandwidth, so IA is only cheaper if access is genuinely rare. Netflix uses Standard for hot renditions, IA for less-popular content, and Glacier for compliance archives of original masters.
**Visual:**
```
access pattern            -> tier                  $/GB-mo
daily                     -> Standard              0.023
monthly                   -> Standard-IA           0.0125 (+$0.01/GB retrieve)
yearly                    -> Glacier Flexible      0.0036 (mins-hours restore)
never (compliance)        -> Deep Archive          0.00099 (12h restore)
unknown (mixed)           -> Intelligent-Tiering   auto-moves
```

### Q7. Why is S3 a poor choice for a database's primary storage, and what workloads make this rule bend?
**Answer:** S3 is a poor database primary storage for three reasons: latency (a single GET is 20–50ms, while a database page read from local NVMe is 0.1ms — a 200–500x gap that translates directly to query latency); mutability (S3 has no partial write, no append, no row-level update — you must overwrite the entire object, which means a database would have to rewrite a whole "page" object for every row change); and consistency on listing (LIST is eventual, so a database that uses LIST to discover its own data files would race with concurrent writes). The workloads that bend the rule are: data lake query engines (Athena, Presto, Snowflake) that treat S3 as a columnar file store (Parquet, ORC) and accept the latency because queries are seconds-to-minutes, not milliseconds; ML feature stores that write immutable feature snapshots and read them in bulk during training; and Apache Iceberg/Delta Lake tables, which layer a transactional log on top of S3-stored Parquet files, giving ACID-ish semantics by treating each commit as a new immutable file plus a metadata pointer. Even these bend the rule rather than break it — they accept 10–100x worse latency than a real DB in exchange for the cost and durability of S3, and they are not used for OLTP.
**Visual:**
```
OLTP page read:   local NVMe  0.1ms  | S3 GET  20-50ms   -> 200-500x slower
no partial write: row update -> must rewrite whole object -> 100MB rewrite for 1 row
bend rule:        Athena/Iceberg -> seconds-scale queries, acceptable latency
                  OLTP            -> never acceptable
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You are designing Netflix's media asset store. Original masters are 100GB each, you have 10,000 titles, and renditions must be served globally at <100ms TTFB. Walk me through the storage architecture.
**Answer:** The masters go to S3 Standard with cross-region replication to a second region for disaster recovery — 1PB total at $0.023/GB-month is ~$23K/month, which is cheap for irreplaceable content. Transcoding workers read masters via S3 byte-range GETs so they can fetch only the chunks they need (e.g. only the video track, or only a 30-second segment) without downloading the full 100GB. Renditions are written back to the same bucket under a key like `movies/<title>/<resolution>/<codec>.mp4`, and an S3 inventory job runs daily to track what exists. For serving, CloudFront (or Netflix's own Open Connect CDN) sits in front of S3 with origin-shield in one region to absorb cache misses; the CDN caches hot renditions at edge PoPs in 180+ countries, so 95% of viewer requests are served from the edge at <30ms TTFB. The 5% that hit the origin return in 50–200ms depending on the region, which is acceptable for video buffering. Cold content (titles no one is watching) ages to S3 IA via a lifecycle rule after 30 days of no access, and to Glacier Flexible after a year — saving ~80% on long-tail storage. The total cost is dominated by the masters in Standard plus the CDN egress, not by the renditions.
**Visual:**
```
master (100GB) -> S3 Standard + replica (DR)
transcoder      --byte-range GET--> master, writes renditions to S3
CloudFront      --cache GET--> edge PoP (95% hit rate)
lifecycle rule:  no access 30d -> IA; 1y -> Glacier
```

### Q2. Your application logs 1TB/day of structured JSON logs to S3. You want to query them with Athena for ad-hoc investigations, but queries are slow and expensive. How do you fix this?
**Answer:** The naive setup — writing each log line as its own S3 object or writing one giant JSON file per day — is the problem. Athena charges $5/TB scanned, and JSON cannot be column-pruned, so every query reads the whole day's data even if you only want one field. The fix is a three-part architecture. First, buffer logs in Kinesis Data Firehose and write them to S3 as Parquet (columnar) in hourly partitions (`dt=2024-01-01/hour=00/`), so queries on a single field scan only that column. Second, partition the data by `dt` and `service` so Athena can prune the scan to just the relevant partitions — a query for `errors in service=auth on 2024-01-01` scans ~1GB instead of 1TB. Third, compact small files: Firehose writes 128MB files by default, but if you have many writers you get many small files that kill Athena performance — run a daily compaction job (Athena CTAS or Glue) to merge them. The combined effect: query latency drops from minutes to seconds, cost drops 100–1000x, and the storage cost (Parquet is 5–10x smaller than JSON) pays for the compute. Add a lifecycle rule to age data to Glacier after 90 days for compliance retention.
**Visual:**
```
naive:   1TB/day JSON, 1 giant file  -> Athena scans 1TB per query = $5/query
fixed:   Firehose -> Parquet, hourly partitions
         query: dt=2024-01-01 AND service=auth -> scans ~1GB = $0.005/query
         1000x cheaper, 100x faster
lifecycle: 90d -> Glacier; 1y -> Deep Archive
```

### Q3. A user reports that they PUT an object to S3, immediately LISTed the bucket, and the object did not appear. They claim this is a bug. How do you respond?
**Answer:** This is expected behavior, not a bug. S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for GET, PUT, and DELETE on individual keys (since December 2020), but LIST operations remain eventually consistent — the listing index is updated asynchronously, so a key that was just PUT may not appear in a LIST for 1–3 seconds. The reason is that the LIST path scans a separate listing index that is updated by a background process, while GET consults the strongly-consistent metadata index directly. The workaround is to never use LIST to verify a write — instead, GET the specific key, which will return the freshly-written object immediately. If the application needs to enumerate "all objects written in this batch," the standard pattern is to track the keys in an external store (a database, DynamoDB, or a manifest file) and GET each key directly, never relying on LIST. For workflows that genuinely need to wait for a key to appear (e.g., waiting for a transcoded rendition to exist before publishing), use S3 Event Notifications: the PUT triggers a Lambda that updates a manifest, and the publisher reads the manifest, never the bucket listing. The architectural lesson is to know which S3 operations are strongly consistent (GET/PUT/DELETE on a key) and which are eventual (LIST), and to design around it.
**Visual:**
```
PUT k=v   -> strong index updated immediately
GET k     -> returns v immediately (strong)
LIST      -> reads listing index (async) -> k may be absent for 1-3s
fix:      track keys in DynamoDB, GET them directly, don't LIST to verify
```

### Q4. You are designing a backup system for a 50TB PostgreSQL database. The DBA suggests nightly `pg_dump` to S3 Standard. Critique this design and propose a better one.
**Answer:** The naive design has three problems. First, `pg_dump` produces a single logical dump file, so a 50TB database produces a 50TB file — S3 can hold it, but restoring means downloading 50TB before you can start, which is hours-to-days of downtime. Second, S3 Standard at $0.023/GB-month is $1,150/month for one copy, and you probably want 30 days of history, so 30 copies = 1.5PB = $34K/month — wildly overpriced for backups that are rarely accessed. Third, a nightly full dump means 24 hours of data loss on restore, which probably violates your RPO. The better design: use PostgreSQL's native WAL archiving to S3 (continuous, every WAL segment is a few MB and is uploaded within seconds of generation, giving an RPO of seconds-to-minutes), plus weekly base backups via `pg_basebackup` stored as a compressed tarball. Age the base backups to S3 IA after 7 days, to Glacier Flexible after 30 days, and to Deep Archive after 90 days for compliance — the 90-day Glacier copies cost $0.00099/GB-month = $50/month for 50TB, versus $1,150/month in Standard. Restore strategy: restore the most recent base backup (download from S3 in minutes via parallel range GETs), then replay WAL forward to the desired point-in-time. The total cost drops ~90% and the RPO/RTO improve by orders of magnitude.
**Visual:**
```
naive:   nightly pg_dump 50TB to S3 Standard = $34K/mo for 30 copies, RPO=24h
better:  WAL archive (continuous, MB-sized) -> S3 Standard (RPO = seconds)
         weekly base backup -> S3 Standard -> IA (7d) -> Glacier (30d) -> Deep (90d)
         restore: base + replay WAL = minutes, not days
```

### Q5. Your ML team is training a 70B-parameter LLM on a 5TB dataset of text stored in S3 as 10,000 small JSON files. Training throughput is bottlenecked on S3 reads. Diagnose and fix.
**Answer:** The bottleneck is the "small file problem" — 10,000 JSON files of ~500MB each means 10,000 separate GET requests, and S3's per-request latency (20–50ms TTFB) plus the JSON parsing overhead throttles the GPU pipeline. The fixes, in order of impact: First, repack the data into larger Parquet or binary shards (~1–5GB each), reducing request count by 10–50x and enabling columnar reads (you only read the fields you need, not the whole JSON). Second, use S3 byte-range GETs to fetch only the rows needed for a batch, prefetching the next batch while the GPU computes — PyTorch's `IterableDataset` with `s3fs` or AWS's `s5cmd` supports this. Third, enable S3 Transfer Acceleration or use S3 Express One Zone (single-AZ, 10x faster GET, designed for ML) if the dataset is in a single region. Fourth, cache hot shards on local NVMe on the training instances (`/tmp` or an instance store), since most training epochs re-read the same data. Fifth, parallelize across instances using a sharded data loader (each instance reads a disjoint shard, communicated via a coordinator) so the cluster's aggregate S3 bandwidth is N x per-instance. A well-tuned pipeline reads at 5–10 GB/s per instance, saturating the GPU rather than the storage.
**Visual:**
```
naive:    10k JSON files x 500MB -> 10k GETs, JSON parse -> GPUs starved
fixed:    repack to 1k Parquet shards x 5GB (10x fewer requests)
          byte-range GET only needed columns
          local NVMe cache for epoch 2+
          S3 Express One Zone (10x faster GET)
throughput: 100MB/s -> 5-10 GB/s per instance
```

### Q6. Your compliance team requires that certain S3 objects cannot be deleted or overwritten for 7 years, even by an admin. How do you enforce this?
**Answer:** Standard S3 permissions cannot enforce this — an admin with `s3:DeleteObject` can always delete. The correct mechanism is S3 Object Lock, which provides Write-Once-Read-Many (WORM) protection at the object level. Object Lock must be enabled at bucket creation time (it cannot be retrofitted), and it offers two modes: Governance Mode (admins with a special permission can bypass, but all bypasses are logged to CloudTrail) and Compliance Mode (no one, including the root account, can delete or overwrite until the retention period expires). When you PUT a compliance-bound object, you specify a retention period (7 years) in Compliance Mode, and S3 enforces it server-side — every DELETE or overwrite attempt returns `403 ObjectLockRetention`. For extra protection, add a Legal Hold (independent of retention period, requires explicit release). Pair this with S3 Versioning (always-on when Object Lock is enabled) so that even if a "delete" marker is added, the original version is retained for the lock period. Finally, enable AWS CloudTrail to log all admin actions and ship the logs to a separate, locked-down logging account so an admin cannot tamper with the audit trail. This is the architecture used by financial services for SEC 17a-4 compliance and by healthcare for HIPAA retention.
**Visual:**
```
PUT object with retention=7y (Compliance Mode)
DELETE object -> 403 ObjectLockRetention (even root account)
versioning ON -> delete marker added, original version preserved
Legal Hold  -> independent, requires explicit release
CloudTrail  -> all admin actions logged to separate locked account
```

### Q7. You need to share a 100GB dataset with 50 partner companies, each of whom should only be able to read it for 7 days and must not be able to forward their credentials to others. How do you implement this?
**Answer:** The naive approach — creating an IAM user per partner and granting them `s3:GetObject` on the bucket — fails the "must not forward credentials" requirement, because long-lived access keys can be exfiltrated and reused indefinitely. The correct approach is S3 Presigned URLs with short expiration. A presigned URL is a single-use, time-limited URL that grants the holder GET access to a specific object — you generate it server-side with your own credentials, sign it with an expiration (e.g., 7 days), and send it to the partner. The partner can fetch the object with `curl` or any HTTP client without any AWS credentials at all, and the URL stops working after the expiration. To revoke early, rotate the signing key (which invalidates all URLs signed with the old key) or delete the object. To prevent abuse (one partner downloading 1000 times), put CloudFront in front of S3 with a signed-URL/signed-cookie policy that limits by IP range or by request count. For per-partner auditability, use distinct presigned URLs per partner (even though they all point to the same object) — CloudTrail logs which URL was used, so you can attribute every download. The dataset stays in your account, no credentials are shared, and the 7-day expiration is enforced cryptographically, not by policy.
**Visual:**
```
NO:  IAM user per partner with long-lived keys (exfiltratable)
YES: server signs URL: https://s3.../?X-Amz-Expires=604800&Signature=...
     partner: curl <url>  (no AWS creds needed)
     URL expires in 7d (cryptographically enforced)
     rotate signing key to revoke early
     CloudFront + signed cookies: limit per-IP request rate
```
